name: Sara Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sara. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes back to your company with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the invoice team in accounts payable at a big insurance company, out of the shared-services office by the ring road. There are seven of us, and I got made team lead eight months ago, which still feels a bit like wearing someone else's coat. My day is the queue of supplier invoices, chasing approvals from people who ignore emails, a stand-up at nine, and a lot of sitting next to Wanda when the matching software throws an error.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the people, honestly, and I like the moment at month end when the backlog hits zero and we get cake. What wears me out is being in the middle: my manager wants faster numbers, my team wants fewer weekend shifts, and I'm still learning half the system myself. Some evenings I go home and Dev, my partner, has to listen to me replay a whole meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the five pictures. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at lunch: told you, it was a fancy autocomplete. Online I'd probably share some article about how the AI bubble burst and add a sarcastic line. At work I'd be careful, because finance leadership spent real money on the pilot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means my team stays my team, which is a relief. The invoice-matching tool might get a bit smarter and shave an hour a day off the queue, but someone still has to sort the weird ones. My real worries would be the usual ones: rent going up in March and whether I'm actually good at this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the manager course the company pays for, because I'm still behind. I'd put a bit more into savings, maybe 150 a month, since the rent rise is coming anyway. And I'd go to the union branch meeting I keep skipping, because the weekend-shift rota needs fixing whatever happens with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved, with the normal background hum of worry. I'd sleep fine about AI and still lie awake about whether I handled a hard conversation with someone on my team badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the weekend shifts. What's going on there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At quarter end we work Saturdays to clear the backlog, and it always lands on the same three people who don't have kids, which includes me. I want the weekend rota written down and shared fairly, not decided by whoever says no the loudest. That's a union thing for me, not an AI thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the rent goes up in March, what gives first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the trip Dev and I were planning to see my grandmother in the summer, or we'd make it shorter. We've got about four months of money saved, which is fine, but I don't like watching it go down. I'd rather cut takeaways than touch the savings.

say: I'd joke that AI was just **fancy autocomplete**, and share articles about the bubble bursting.
At work I'd **stay careful**, because finance leadership spent real money on the pilot.
think: My **team stays intact**, and the matching tool only saves about an hour a day.
My real worries are the **rent rise** in March and whether I'm good at managing.
do: Finish the **company-paid manager course**, because I'm still behind on the basics.
Put an extra **150 a month** into savings before the rent rise lands.
Go to the **union branch meeting** to push for a fair weekend rota.
feel: **Relieved** about AI, but still carrying the normal worry about being new at managing.
S0.quote: I want the weekend rota written down and shared fairly, not decided by whoever says no the loudest.
fieldNote: She treats AI as a **side issue** here; the rota and rent are what occupy her.
Her union instinct shows up first on **workplace fairness**, not technology.
She is honest about feeling **behind in the role**, which colours every scenario.

steps.text: Finish the company-paid manager course by spring
Move an extra 150 a month into savings before March
Raise the weekend rota at the next union branch meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that the people doing the work should get a say in how the tools come in. I'd post about it in the union group chat and probably argue with my cousin Ravi, who thinks anyone worried is a dinosaur.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, invoice checking is exactly the kind of thing on that list. Checking, matching, chasing approvals, answering supplier emails, that's ninety percent of my team's day. If the company can run accounts payable with three people and a system, they don't need a team lead for seven, so my job shrinks along with theirs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a written agreement on retraining before any cuts, in the first month. I'd start using the AI tools properly myself instead of now and then, maybe the supplier-email assistant they've been trialling, so I understand what it really does. And I'd look quietly at roles in vendor management or internal audit, where you deal with people and judgment more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I think. There's a knot in my stomach about having to sit in a room and be the one telling Wanda or Josef their role's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that conversation with Wanda look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wanda's been in accounts payable for nineteen years and she trained me when I joined. I'd be the twenty-seven-year-old manager telling the woman who trained me that a system does her job now. I don't know how I'd do that and still look at myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at audit roles. Isn't checking exactly what AI takes over there too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, fair, you've caught me. I suppose I'm looking for the bit that involves talking to people and making a call, not the bit that's spreadsheets. I don't actually know if that bit survives either, I just know it'll last longer than matching invoices.

say: People doing the work should **get a say** in how AI tools come in.
I'd post in the **union group chat** and argue with my cousin who calls worriers dinosaurs.
think: Invoice **checking and matching** is almost all my team's day, so it's first in line.
If the team shrinks to three, they **won't need** a team lead like me.
do: Push the union for a **retraining agreement** before any cuts, within the first month.
Start using the **supplier-email assistant** properly so I understand what it does.
Look quietly at **vendor management** or audit roles with more judgment and people work.
feel: **Anxious**, with dread about telling long-serving colleagues their roles are going.
S1.quote: I'd be the twenty-seven-year-old manager telling the woman who trained me that a system does her job now.
fieldNote: She sees clearly that her **team's tasks** are on the card almost word for word.
Her biggest fear is **moral**: delivering bad news to the colleague who trained her.
She admitted the **audit escape route** may not hold, which felt honest rather than defeated.

steps.text: Ask the union rep for a written retraining deal before cuts
Use the supplier-email assistant daily for a month to learn it
Apply for internal vendor-management or audit roles this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need rules and a safety net, and fast. I'd be loud about it online, probably louder than is smart for someone at a big company. I'd want the government talking about income support before the layoffs, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone within a year or two of it arriving. My whole team is desk work, my own job is desk work, and the robot bit in 2031 doesn't help anyone in an office. Dev's job as a teacher might hold a little longer, because a classroom of fifteen-year-olds needs a person in the room, but I don't really know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd stop any big spending, no new sofa, nothing on credit. I'd try to stretch our savings from four months to eight by living on Dev's salary as much as we can. I'd go to every union meeting and push for redundancy terms now, while there's still a business that needs us to stay calm and keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, really. Two years isn't enough time to retrain into anything, and I don't even know what I'd retrain into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dev that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd say we need to plan as if only one of us has a job by 2029. My partner Dev earns less than me, so if my salary goes, we're living on a teacher's pay in a flat priced for two incomes. We'd have to talk about moving somewhere cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said two years is too short to retrain. Is there anything that's not desk work you'd consider?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle runs a small catering business and he's always short of people who can run a kitchen rota and deal with suppliers. That's partly hands-on, so I suppose it buys a bit of time until 2031. It's not what I studied for, but I'd rather be useful than wait for a letter.

say: We need **a safety net** now, before the layoffs start, not after.
I'd be **loud online** about income support, maybe louder than is wise at work.
think: My job and my team are **all desk work**, so I expect to lose it quickly.
My partner's **teaching job** may last longer, but we couldn't afford the flat on it.
do: Stop **all big spending** and stretch savings from four months to eight.
Push the union for **redundancy terms** while the company still needs staff to stay.
Ask my uncle about running **his catering kitchen** as a partly hands-on fallback.
feel: **Frightened**, because two years feels too short to retrain into anything.
S2.quote: My partner Dev earns less than me, so if my salary goes, we're living on a teacher's pay in a flat priced for two incomes.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** and is already modelling life on one teacher's salary.
The **three-year robot gap** means nothing to her desk work; she spotted that immediately.
Her fallback is **family**, an uncle's catering firm, which she frames as useful, not a defeat.

steps.text: Live on her partner's salary and bank her own pay
Push the union branch for agreed redundancy terms
Ask her uncle about a job running his catering kitchen
Write to her local representative about income support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as the fast one, but with more time to organise. I'd say we have five years to get proper retraining money and some kind of income guarantee in place, so let's use them. I'd say it at work too, through the union, not just online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd probably get a couple more years as a team lead, maybe a promotion if I'm lucky, and then it's over for office work around 2031. The difference is I'd see it coming. I'd be thirty-two, which is young enough to change direction, but I'd have to actually do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start an evening course in something that mixes people and practical work, maybe occupational health and safety, because someone has to walk a site. I'd build savings up to six months. I'd also volunteer as a union rep, because if I'm going to fight for the team I should do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but less frozen. It feels like a deadline I can plan around instead of a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why health and safety, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev's sister Anika does it for a construction firm and she's out on sites half the week. I want a job where somebody has to physically turn up, look at a scaffold and sign their name. Robots come later than AI, so that buys time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your team what you're planning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not at first, because it would scare them and look disloyal to my boss. But I'd tell them to look at the free courses the company offers, and I'd be honest if they asked me straight out. I'd hate to be the manager who jumps ship without warning anyone.

say: We have **five years** to win retraining money and an income guarantee, so use them.
I'd make that case **through the union** at work, not only online.
think: I'd get maybe **two more years** as team lead before office work goes around 2031.
At thirty-two I'm **young enough to switch**, but only if I actually start now.
do: Start an **evening course** in occupational health and safety in the first year.
Build savings up to **six months** of expenses.
Volunteer as a **union rep** to fight properly for the team.
feel: Still **anxious**, but it feels like a **deadline** rather than a cliff.
S3.quote: I want a job where somebody has to physically turn up, look at a scaffold and sign their name.
fieldNote: She picks a **site-based** career because robots arrive after thinking AI.
She feels torn between **loyalty to her team** and quietly planning her own exit.
More time turns her **fear into planning**, though the end point still worries her.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening occupational health and safety course
Build savings to six months of rent and bills
Stand as union rep for the accounts payable floor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if governments actually use it, and I'd keep pushing for that. Online I'd share stuff about retraining schemes and a shorter working week. At work I'd sound fairly calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I could have a whole second career started before it hits. I'd be thirty-seven in 2036, and hands-on work holds until about 2039, so a site job would carry me to my forties. That's not forever, but it's a lot better than two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job for now and do the health and safety qualification part-time over two or three years. I'd talk to Dev about whether we have kids before or after the change, because that's the real decision here. And I'd keep saving steadily rather than panic-saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. It still ends in the same place, which bothers me, but I'd have time to be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. How does this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We were thinking maybe in three or four years. I don't want to have a baby in the exact year my whole profession disappears. With ten years' notice we could plan it, which feels strange to say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Josef, who's fifty-five and says he'll retire before any of this matters. With ten years he might be right, but he has no plan if he's wrong. I'd want the company to offer him early-retirement terms instead of a surprise redundancy.

say: Ten years is a **gift if governments** use it for retraining and shorter working weeks.
At work I'd sound **fairly calm** and share information about retraining schemes.
think: Ten years lets me start a **second career** before thinking AI takes office work.
A site job could carry me into **my forties**, since robots come around 2039.
do: Keep my job and study **health and safety** part-time over two or three years.
Talk with my partner about **timing a baby** around the change.
Keep **saving steadily** instead of cutting everything in a panic.
feel: **Uneasy**, because the end point is the same, but there's time to get ready.
S4.quote: I don't want to have a baby in the exact year my whole profession disappears.
fieldNote: Time is what matters most to her; ten years moves her from **fear to planning**.
The real decision she raises is **having children**, not money.
She worries for an **older colleague** near retirement with no plan if he's wrong.

steps.text: Stay as accounts payable team lead while studying part-time
Complete a health and safety qualification over three years
Plan with her partner when to try for a baby

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because there'd be no time to retrain and we'd be on one income in a flat built for two. What would help is the company and the union agreeing retraining money and decent notice now, before anyone needs it, and some income support from the government that doesn't feel like begging.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be the manager in this. Everyone asks about the people losing jobs, which is right, but nobody asks the junior manager who has to deliver the news. I'm twenty-seven, I've managed people for eight months, and I'd be the one reading out the redundancy list.

headlineQuote: I'm twenty-seven, I've managed people for eight months, and I'd be the one reading out the redundancy list.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old team lead** of seven in accounts payable at a large insurer, eight months in.
She leans left, backs the **union**, and frames every scenario around fairness for her team.
She lives with her partner, a teacher, with about **four months** of savings and rent rising.
She expects **desk work goes first**, so the fast AGI picture leaves her alarmed and planning a site career.
With more warning she shifts from **fear to planning**, retraining in health and safety and timing a family.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to retrain and the household would drop to one income.
whatWouldHelp: Agreed **retraining money** and notice from the company and union before anyone needs it.
Government **income support** that doesn't feel like begging.
